title: Both views wrongly confuse the free with the voluntary
source_text: XX. In utraque autem istud incommodi est quod omnino confundunt liberum & voluntarium, & statuunt omnes actus voluntatis liberos esse. Nam juxta sensum communem hominum, & receptum loquendi usum, istud solum liberum nobis esse dicitur, quod in nostra potestate est, quod potest aliter se habere, & de quo nobis consultare & deliberare licet. Jam vero, ut supra ostendimus, sunt quidam voluntatis actus, ad quos per naturam sic determinata est, ut nullo modo possint aliter se habere, & de quibus nulla potest institui deliberatio. Adde quod omnes actus qui a nobis libere procedunt possunt praeceptis quibusdam subjacere, & lege aliqua divina, vel humana mandari, sive prohiberi. Istud autem nullo modo convenit iis actibus circa quos voluntas plane immutabiliter se habet, ita ut in nullo statu potuerit, vel possit unquam aliter agere. Denique cum illi quibuscum nobis res est, fateantur & agnoscant magnum discrimen esse inter actus voluntatis, nempe quosdam sic esse in nostra potestate, ut de iis possimus consultare & deliberare; illosque pro vario mentis practicae judicio, vel facere, vel omittere, aut etiam contrarium agere; aliorum vero plane diversam esse rationem; cur nolunt res natura distinctas, distinctis quoque vocibus signare, & juxta usum in Scholis receptum illis quidem liberi, his vero voluntarii nomen appropriare? cum sapientis sit sine necessitate a communi loquendi modo non recedere.
pass_a_gloss: But in both there is this inconvenience that they altogether confound the free & the voluntary, & state all acts of the will to be free. For according to the common sense of men, & the received use of speaking, that alone is said to be free to us, which is in our power, which can be otherwise, & about which it is permitted to us to consult & deliberate. Now, as we showed above, there are certain acts of the will, to which it is so determined by nature, that they can in no way be otherwise, & about which no deliberation can be set up. Add that all acts which proceed freely from us can be subject to certain precepts, & be commanded, or forbidden by some divine, or human law. But this in no way suits those acts about which the will holds itself plainly immutably, so that in no state could it, or can it ever act otherwise. Finally since those with whom we have to do, confess & acknowledge that there is a great difference between acts of the will, namely that some are so in our power, that we can consult & deliberate about them; and either do, or omit them according to the various judgement of the practical mind, or even do the contrary; but that of others the nature is plainly different; why will they not mark things distinct by nature, with distinct words also, & according to the use received in the Schools appropriate to those indeed the name of free, but to these of voluntary? since it is the part of a wise man not to depart without necessity from the common mode of speaking.
pass_b_english: Both views share one drawback: they wholly confuse the free with the voluntary and hold that every act of the will is free. In the common understanding of men and in ordinary usage, we call free only what is in our power, what could be otherwise, and what we are allowed to weigh and deliberate about.

But as shown above, there are acts of the will to which it is so fixed by nature that they cannot be otherwise in any way, and about which no deliberation can be held. Further, every act that comes from us freely can fall under precepts and be commanded or forbidden by some law, divine or human. That does not fit at all the acts toward which the will stands quite unchangeably, so that in no state could it, or ever can it, act otherwise.

Lastly, the men we are dealing with admit a great difference among the will's acts. Some are in our power, so that we can weigh and deliberate about them and, as the practical mind judges one way or another, do them, leave them undone, or even do the opposite; the others are of a quite different kind. Why, then, will they not give things that differ in nature different names too, and, following the usage of the schools, reserve 'free' for the first and 'voluntary' for the second? A wise man does not leave the common way of speaking without need.

choices.english: the men we are dealing with
choices.why: The idiom names one's opponents in a dispute; here the Reformed writers just discussed.
rejected: those with whom we have business
